claim: Exome sequencing on tens of thousands of parent-proband trios has identified numerous deleterious de novo mutations (DNMs) and implicated risk genes for many disorders.
source: Exome sequencing on tens of thousands of parent-proband trios has identified numerous deleterious de novo mutations (DNMs) and implicated risk genes for many disorders.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on DNM studies.

claim: Recent studies have suggested shared genes and pathways are enriched for DNMs across multiple disorders.
source: Recent studies have suggested shared genes and pathways are enriched for DNMs across multiple disorders.
evidence: Supported by references to recent literature on shared genetic architecture.

claim: Existing analytic strategies only focus on genes that reach statistical significance for multiple disorders and require large trio samples in each study.
source: However, existing analytic strategies only focus on genes that reach statistical significance for multiple disorders and require large trio samples in each study.
evidence: Based on characterization of current methodological approaches in the field.

claim: Existing methods are not able to characterize the full landscape of genetic sharing due to polygenicity and incomplete penetrance.
source: As a result, these methods are not able to characterize the full landscape of genetic sharing due to polygenicity and incomplete penetrance.
evidence: Logical inference about limitations of current methods based on biological complexity.

claim: EncoreDNM is a novel statistical framework to quantify shared genetic effects between two disorders characterized by concordant enrichment of DNMs in the exome.
source: In this work, we introduce EncoreDNM, a novel statistical framework to quantify shared genetic effects between two disorders characterized by concordant enrichment of DNMs in the exome.
evidence: Direct statement of the method introduced in this manuscript.

claim: EncoreDNM makes use of exome-wide, summary-level DNM data, including genes that do not reach statistical significance in single-disorder analysis.
source: EncoreDNM makes use of exome-wide, summary-level DNM data, including genes that do not reach statistical significance in single-disorder analysis, to evaluate the overall and annotation-partitioned genetic sharing between two disorders.
evidence: Description of the method's input data and approach.

claim: Applying EncoreDNM to DNM data of nine disorders identified abundant pairwise enrichment correlations.
source: Applying EncoreDNM to DNM data of nine disorders, we identified abundant pairwise enrichment correlations, especially in genes intolerant to pathogenic mutations and genes highly expressed in fetal tissues.
evidence: Results from applying the method to real data.

claim: Enrichment correlations are especially strong in genes intolerant to pathogenic mutations and genes highly expressed in fetal tissues.
source: Applying EncoreDNM to DNM data of nine disorders, we identified abundant pairwise enrichment correlations, especially in genes intolerant to pathogenic mutations and genes highly expressed in fetal tissues.
evidence: Specific findings from the analysis of nine disorders.

claim: De novo mutations (DNMs) can be highly deleterious and provide important insights into the genetic cause for disease.
source: De novo mutations (DNMs) can be highly deleterious and provide important insights into the genetic cause for disease (Veltman and Brunner, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) studies conducted on tens of thousands of family trios have pinpointed numerous risk genes for a variety of disorders.
source: As the cost of sequencing continues to drop, whole-exome sequencing (WES) studies conducted on tens of thousands of family trios have pinpointed numerous risk genes for a variety of disorders (Lelieveld et al., 2016; Kaplanis et al., 2020; Satterstrom et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to large-scale WES studies.

claim: Risk genes enriched for pathogenic DNMs may be shared by multiple disorders.
source: In addition, accumulating evidence suggests that risk genes enriched for pathogenic DNMs may be shared by multiple disorders (Hoischen et al., 2014; Fromer et al., 2014; Homsy et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies showing shared genetic architecture.

claim: Shared genes could reveal biological pathways that play prominent roles in disease etiology.
source: These shared genes could reveal biological pathways that play prominent roles in disease etiology and shed light on clinically heterogeneous yet genetically related diseases (Homsy et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference about the biological significance of shared genes, supported by citations.

claim: Most efforts to identify shared risk genes directly compare genes that are significantly associated with each disorder.
source: Most efforts to identify shared risk genes directly compare genes that are significantly associated with each disorder (Nguyen et al., 2017; Willsey et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of current methodological approaches, supported by citations.

claim: There have been some successes in identifying shared genes and pathways (e.g. chromatin modifiers) underlying developmental disorder (DD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and congenital heart disease (CHD).
source: There have been some successes with this approach in identifying shared genes and pathways (e.g. chromatin modifiers) underlying developmental disorder (DD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and congenital heart disease (CHD), thanks to the large trio samples in these studies (Kaplanis et al., 2020; Satterstrom et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2017), whereas findings in smaller studies remain suggestive (Allen et al., 2013; Jin et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citations to specific studies showing shared pathways.

claim: Statistical power remains moderate for risk genes with weaker effects even in the largest studies to date.
source: Even in the largest studies to date, statistical power remains moderate for risk genes with weaker effects (Kaplanis et al., 2020; Howrigan et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to large-scale studies discussing power limitations.

claim: More than 1000 haploinsufficient genes contributing to developmental disorder risk have not yet achieved statistical significance in large WES studies.
source: It is estimated that more than 1000 haploinsufficient genes contributing to developmental disorder risk have not yet achieved statistical significance in large WES studies (Kaplanis et al., 2020).
evidence: Specific estimate from a cited study.

claim: Analytic approaches that only account for top significant genes cannot capture the full landscape of genetic sharing in multiple disorders.
source: Therefore, analytic approaches that only account for top significant genes cannot capture the full landscape of genetic sharing in multiple disorders.
evidence: Logical inference based on the limitations of current methods and incomplete power.

claim: mTADA is a Bayesian framework that was proposed to jointly analyze DNM data of two diseases and improve risk gene mapping.
source: Recently, a Bayesian framework named mTADA was proposed to jointly analyze DNM data of two diseases and improve risk gene mapping (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of an existing method, supported by citation.

claim: The statistical property of mTADA's parameter estimates has not been studied.
source: Although mTADA produces estimates for the proportion of shared risk genes, the statistical property of these parameter estimates has not been studied.
evidence: Statement about a gap in the characterization of an existing method.

claim: There is a pressing need for powerful, robust, and interpretable methods that quantify concordant DNM association patterns for multiple disorders using exome-wide DNM counts.
source: There is a pressing need for powerful, robust, and interpretable methods that quantify concordant DNM association patterns for multiple disorders using exome-wide DNM counts.
evidence: Statement of the motivation for developing the new method.

claim: Linear mixed-effects models leverage genome-wide association profiles to quantify the correlation between additive genetic components of multiple complex traits.
source: Modeling 'omnigenic' associations as independent random effects, linear mixed-effects models leverage genome-wide association profiles to quantify the correlation between additive genetic components of multiple complex traits (Lee et al., 2012; Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2017; Ning et al., 2020).
evidence: Description of existing GWAS methods, supported by multiple citations.

claim: GWAS genetic correlation methods have identified ubiquitous genetic correlations across many human traits.
source: These methods have identified ubiquitous genetic correlations across many human traits and revealed significant and robust genetic correlations that could not be inferred from significant GWAS associations alone (Shi et al., 2017; Brainstorm, 2018; Guo et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating widespread genetic correlations.

claim: EncoreDNM uses a generalized linear mixed-effects model to quantify the occurrence of DNMs while accounting for de novo mutability of each gene and technical inconsistencies between studies.
source: EncoreDNM uses a generalized linear mixed-effects model to quantify the occurrence of DNMs while accounting for de novo mutability of each gene and technical inconsistencies between studies.
evidence: Description of the statistical model used in the method.

claim: DNM counts in the exome deviate from the null when mutations play a role in disease etiology.
source: DNM counts in the exome deviate from the null (i.e. expected counts based on de novo mutability) when mutations play a role in disease etiology.
evidence: Conceptual statement about the biological basis of the method.

claim: Disease risk genes will show enrichment for deleterious DNMs in probands.
source: Disease risk genes will show enrichment for deleterious DNMs in probands and non-risk genes may be slightly depleted for DNM counts.
evidence: Expected pattern based on biological understanding of disease genetics.

claim: Non-risk genes may be slightly depleted for DNM counts.
source: Disease risk genes will show enrichment for deleterious DNMs in probands and non-risk genes may be slightly depleted for DNM counts.
evidence: Expected pattern based on biological understanding and potential selection effects.

claim: Batch effect caused by different sequencing and variant calling pipelines is an example of systematic bias in DNM counts.
source: One example of such bias is the batch effect caused by different sequencing and variant calling pipelines in two studies.
evidence: Specific example of technical bias in sequencing studies.

claim: EncoreDNM provided unbiased estimation of parameters under various parameter settings in simulations.
source: Under various parameter settings, EncoreDNM always provided unbiased estimation of the parameters (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: Simulation results demonstrating unbiased parameter estimation.

claim: The 95% Wald confidence intervals achieved coverage rates close to 95% under all simulation settings.
source: Furthermore, the 95% Wald confidence intervals achieved coverage rates close to 95% under all simulation settings, demonstrating the effectiveness of EncoreDNM to provide accurate statistical inference.
evidence: Simulation results showing proper calibration of confidence intervals.

claim: EncoreDNM showed well-controlled false positive rate across all simulation settings.
source: EncoreDNM showed well-controlled false positive rate across all simulation settings, whereas severe inflation of false positives arose for mTADA when the total mutation count, the proportion of probands that can be explained by DNMs, or the sample size were small (Figure 3c).
evidence: Simulation results comparing false positive rates between methods.

claim: mTADA produced false positive findings when the observed DNM counts were relatively small.
source: The false positive rates for our method were well-calibrated in all parameter settings, but mTADA produced false positive findings when the observed DNM counts were relatively small (e.g. due to reduced elevation or dispersion parameters or a lower sample size; Figure 3a).
evidence: Simulation results showing inflated false positives for mTADA.

claim: EncoreDNM achieved universally greater statistical power compared to mTADA as enrichment correlation increased.
source: As enrichment correlation increased, EncoreDNM achieved universally greater statistical power compared to mTADA (Figure 3b).
evidence: Simulation results comparing statistical power between methods.

claim: Negative elevation parameters for LoF variants may be explained by more stringent quality control in LoF variant calling.
source: This may be explained by more stringent quality control in LoF variant calling (Jin et al., 2017) and potential survival bias (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Negative elevation parameters for LoF variants may be explained by potential survival bias.
source: This may be explained by more stringent quality control in LoF variant calling (Jin et al., 2017) and potential survival bias (Lek et al., 2016).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by citation.

claim: There is a depletion of LoF DNMs in healthy control trios.
source: It is also consistent with a depletion of LoF DNMs in healthy control trios (Homsy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to a study of control trios.

claim: The mixed-effects Poisson model showed substantial and statistically significant improvement in goodness of fit compared to a simpler fixed-effects model.
source: The expected distribution of recurrent DNM counts showed substantial and statistically significant improvement under the mixed-effects Poisson model (Figure 4c–f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1-STable 2).
evidence: Statistical comparison of model fit using real data.

claim: 25 pairs of disorders showed significant enrichment correlations at a false discovery rate (FDR) cutoff of 0.05.
source: In total, we identified 25 pairs of disorders with significant correlations at a false discovery rate (FDR) cutoff of 0.05 (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), including 12 significant correlations for LoF variants, 7 for Dmis variants, 5 for Tmis variants, and only 1 significant correlation for synonymous variants.
evidence: Results from pairwise correlation analysis of nine disorders.

claim: All significant enrichment correlations identified are positive.
source: Notably, all significant correlations are positive (Supplementary file 1-STable 3).
evidence: Summary of the direction of significant correlations.

claim: No significant correlation was identified between any disorder and healthy controls.
source: No significant correlation was identified between any disorder and healthy controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Results from analysis comparing disorders to controls.

claim: The number of identified significant correlations for each disorder was proportional to the sample size in each study (Spearman correlation = 0.70).
source: The number of identified significant correlations for each disorder was proportional to the sample size in each study (Spearman correlation = 0.70) with controls being a notable outlier (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing relationship between sample size and number of significant findings.

claim: Highly concordant and significant LoF DNM enrichment was identified among developmental disorder, autism, intellectual disability, and congenital heart disease.
source: We identified highly concordant and significant LoF DNM enrichment among developmental disorder, autism, intellectual disability, and congenital heart disease, which is consistent with previous reports (Li et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2017; Hormozdiari et al., 2015).
evidence: Results from the analysis, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Schizophrenia shows highly significant LoF correlations with developmental disorder (p=2.0e-3) and intellectual disability (3.7e-5).
source: Schizophrenia shows highly significant LoF correlations with developmental disorder (p=2.0e-3) and intellectual disability (3.7e-5).
evidence: Specific statistical results from the analysis.

claim: A previous study suggested significant genetic sharing of intellectual disability and cerebral palsy by overlapping genes harboring rare damaging variants.
source: A previous study also suggested significant genetic sharing of intellectual disability and cerebral palsy by overlapping genes harboring rare damaging variants (Jin et al., 2020b).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Five genes (CTNNB1, NBEA, POGZ, SPRED2, and KMT2C) had LoF DNMs in five different disorders.
source: We identified five genes (CTNNB1, NBEA, POGZ, SPRED2, and KMT2C) with LoF DNMs in five different disorders and 21 genes had LoF DNMs in four disorders (Supplementary file 1-STable 5).
evidence: Results from analysis of genes with DNMs across multiple disorders.

claim: 21 genes had LoF DNMs in four disorders.
source: We identified five genes (CTNNB1, NBEA, POGZ, SPRED2, and KMT2C) with LoF DNMs in five different disorders and 21 genes had LoF DNMs in four disorders (Supplementary file 1-STable 5).
evidence: Results from analysis of genes with DNMs across multiple disorders.

claim: 26 genes with LoF variants in at least four disorders were significantly enriched for 63 gene ontology (GO) terms with FDR <0.05.
source: These 26 genes with LoF variants in at least four disorders were significantly enriched for 63 gene ontology (GO) terms with FDR <0.05 (Supplementary file 1-STable 6).
evidence: Results from gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Chromatin organization (p=7.8e-11) was one of the most significantly enriched GO terms.
source: Chromatin organization (p=7.8e-11), nucleoplasm (p=2.8e-10), chromosome organization (p=6.8e-10), histone methyltransferase complex (p=1.4e-9), and positive regulation of gene expression (p=2.2e-9) were the most significantly enriched GO terms.
evidence: Results from gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: CTNNB1 is a fundamental component of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway which is known to confer genetic risk for autism.
source: It is a fundamental component of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway which is known to confer genetic risk for autism (O'Roak et al., 2012).
evidence: Biological knowledge about pathway function and disease association, supported by citation.

claim: 30 recurrent cross-disorder LoF mutations were identified that were not recurrent in developmental disorder alone.
source: We identified 30 recurrent cross-disorder LoF mutations that were not recurrent in developmental disorder alone (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Results from analysis of recurrent mutations.

claim: FBXO11 shows two recurrent p.Ser831fs LoF variants in autism and congenital hydrocephalus (p=1.9e-3).
source: FBXO11, encoding the F-box only protein 31, shows two recurrent p.Ser831fs LoF variants in autism and congenital hydrocephalus (Figure 5—figure supplement 5; p=1.9e-3; Materials and methods).
evidence: Specific finding about recurrent mutations with statistical significance.

claim: FBXO11 encodes the F-box only protein 31.
source: FBXO11, encoding the F-box only protein 31, shows two recurrent p.Ser831fs LoF variants in autism and congenital hydrocephalus (Figure 5—figure supplement 5; p=1.9e-3; Materials and methods).
evidence: Biological fact about gene function.

claim: The F-box protein constitutes a substrate-recognition component of the SCF (SKP1-cullin-F-box) complex, an E3-ubiquitin ligase complex responsible for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: The F-box protein constitutes a substrate-recognition component of the SCF (SKP1-cullin-F-box) complex, an E3-ubiquitin ligase complex responsible for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Cardozo and Pagano, 2004).
evidence: Biological knowledge about protein function, supported by citation.

claim: DNMs in FBXO11 have been previously implicated in severe intellectual disability individuals with autistic behavior problem.
source: DNMs in FBXO11 have been previously implicated in severe intellectual disability individuals with autistic behavior problem (Jansen et al., 2019) and neurodevelopmental disorder (Gregor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNMs in FBXO11 have been previously implicated in neurodevelopmental disorder.
source: DNMs in FBXO11 have been previously implicated in severe intellectual disability individuals with autistic behavior problem (Jansen et al., 2019) and neurodevelopmental disorder (Gregor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: mTADA identified 117 disorder pairs with significant genetic sharings at an FDR cutoff of 0.05.
source: In total, mTADA identified 117 disorder pairs with significant genetic sharings at an FDR cutoff of 0.05 (Supplementary file 1-STable 8 and Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Results from applying mTADA to the same data.

claim: mTADA identified significant synonymous DNM correlations for all 36 disorder pairs and between all disorders and healthy controls.
source: Notably, we identified significant synonymous DNM correlations for all 36 disorder pairs and between all disorders and healthy controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Results from mTADA analysis showing unexpected findings.

claim: The mTADA results are consistent with the simulation results and suggest a substantially inflated false positive rate in mTADA.
source: These results are consistent with the simulation results and suggest a substantially inflated false positive rate in mTADA.
evidence: Interpretation of mTADA results in light of simulation findings.

claim: 11 disorder pairs showed significant enrichment correlations for LoF DNMs in high-pLI genes.
source: We identified 11 and 12 disorder pairs showing significant enrichment correlations for LoF DNMs in high-pLI genes and HBE genes, respectively (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: Results from gene set-specific analysis.

claim: 12 disorder pairs showed significant enrichment correlations for LoF DNMs in HBE genes.
source: We identified 11 and 12 disorder pairs showing significant enrichment correlations for LoF DNMs in high-pLI genes and HBE genes, respectively (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: Results from gene set-specific analysis.

claim: High-pLI genes showed substantially stronger correlations across disorders than genes with low pLI (one-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; p=2.3e-6).
source: Overall, high-pLI genes showed substantially stronger correlations across disorders than genes with low pLI (one-sided Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; p=2.3e-6).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation strength between gene sets.

claim: Enrichment correlations were stronger in HBE genes than in LBE genes (p=8.8e-7).
source: Similarly, enrichment correlations were stronger in HBE genes than in LBE genes (p=8.8e-7).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation strength between gene sets.

claim: Novel enrichment correlations in HBE genes are consistent with known comorbidities between these disorders.
source: These novel enrichment correlations are consistent with known comorbidities between these disorders (Kielinen et al., 2004; Kilincaslan and Mukaddes, 2009) and findings based on significant risk genes (Li et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2020a; Kume et al., 1998; Cao and Wu, 2015).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by citations to epidemiological and genetic studies.

claim: 9 significant enrichment correlations for LoF variants in HHE genes were identified.
source: We identified 9 significant enrichment correlations for LoF variants in HHE genes (Figure 6c).
evidence: Results from gene set-specific analysis.

claim: Strength of enrichment correlations did not show a significant difference between HHE and LHE genes (p=0.846).
source: Strength of enrichment correlations did not show a significant difference between HHE and LHE genes (p=0.846), possibly due to a lack of cardiac disorders in our analysis.
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation strength between gene sets.

claim: Arrhythmia caused by congenital heart disease is a known risk factor for Tourette disorder.
source: Of note, arrhythmia caused by congenital heart disease is a known risk factor for Tourette disorder (Gulisano et al., 2011).
evidence: Clinical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The mixed-effects Poisson regression model provides unbiased parameter estimates.
source: Through extensive simulations and analyses of DNM data for nine disorders, we demonstrated that our proposed mixed-effects Poisson regression model provides unbiased parameter estimates, shows well-controlled false positive rate, and is robust to exome-wide technical biases.
evidence: Summary of simulation and real data analysis results.

claim: The mixed-effects Poisson regression model shows well-controlled false positive rate.
source: Through extensive simulations and analyses of DNM data for nine disorders, we demonstrated that our proposed mixed-effects Poisson regression model provides unbiased parameter estimates, shows well-controlled false positive rate, and is robust to exome-wide technical biases.
evidence: Summary of simulation and real data analysis results.

claim: The mixed-effects Poisson regression model is robust to exome-wide technical biases.
source: Through extensive simulations and analyses of DNM data for nine disorders, we demonstrated that our proposed mixed-effects Poisson regression model provides unbiased parameter estimates, shows well-controlled false positive rate, and is robust to exome-wide technical biases.
evidence: Summary of simulation and real data analysis results.

claim: EncoreDNM achieves superior fit for real DNM datasets compared to simpler models.
source: Leveraging exome-wide DNM counts and genomic context-based mutability data, EncoreDNM achieves superior fit for real DNM datasets compared to simpler models and provides statistically powerful and computationally efficient estimation of DNM enrichment correlation.
evidence: Results from model comparison using real data.

claim: EncoreDNM provides statistically powerful and computationally efficient estimation of DNM enrichment correlation.
source: Leveraging exome-wide DNM counts and genomic context-based mutability data, EncoreDNM achieves superior fit for real DNM datasets compared to simpler models and provides statistically powerful and computationally efficient estimation of DNM enrichment correlation.
evidence: Summary of method performance characteristics.

claim: EncoreDNM can quantify concordant genetic effects for user-defined variant classes within pre-specified gene sets.
source: Further, EncoreDNM can quantify concordant genetic effects for user-defined variant classes within pre-specified gene sets, thus is suitable for exploring diverse types of hypotheses and can provide crucial biological insights into the shared genetic etiology in multiple disorders.
evidence: Description of method capabilities demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: The Bayesian approach implemented in mTADA can produce false positives findings, especially when the DNM count is low.
source: In comparison, the Bayesian approach implemented in mTADA can produce false positives findings, especially when the DNM count is low, possibility due to the overestimated proportion of risk genes.
evidence: Results from simulation and real data comparison with mTADA.

claim: Multi-trait analyses of GWAS data have revealed shared genetic architecture among many neuropsychiatric traits.
source: Multi-trait analyses of GWAS data have revealed shared genetic architecture among many neuropsychiatric traits (Brainstorm, 2018; Lee et al., 2013; Gratten et al., 2014; Abdellaoui and Verweij, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: GWAS findings have led to the identification of pleiotropic variants, genes, and hub genomic regions underlying many traits.
source: These findings have led to the identification of pleiotropic variants, genes, and hub genomic regions underlying many traits and have revealed multiple psychopathological factors jointly affecting human neurological phenotypes (Lee, 2019; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: Emerging evidence suggests that causal DNMs underlying several disorders with well-powered studies may be shared.
source: Although emerging evidence suggests that causal DNMs underlying several disorders with well-powered studies (e.g. congenital heart disease and neurodevelopmental disorders; Homsy et al., 2015) may be shared, our understanding of the extent and the mechanism underlying such sharing remains incomplete.
evidence: Supported by citation to a study showing shared DNMs.

claim: Our understanding of the extent and the mechanism underlying genetic sharing of DNMs remains incomplete.
source: Although emerging evidence suggests that causal DNMs underlying several disorders with well-powered studies (e.g. congenital heart disease and neurodevelopmental disorders; Homsy et al., 2015) may be shared, our understanding of the extent and the mechanism underlying such sharing remains incomplete.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: EncoreDNM identified pervasive enrichment correlations of DNMs when applied to DNM data for nine disorders.
source: Applied to DNM data for nine disorders, EncoreDNM identified pervasive enrichment correlations of DNMs.
evidence: Summary of results from applying the method to real data.

claim: Particularly strong correlations were observed in pathogenic variant classes (e.g. LoF and Dmis variants) and disease-relevant genes.
source: We observed particularly strong correlations in pathogenic variant classes (e.g. LoF and Dmis variants) and disease-relevant genes (e.g. genes with high pLI and genes highly expressed in relevant tissues).
evidence: Summary of patterns observed in the results.

claim: Genes underlying DNM correlations were significantly enriched in pathways involved in chromatin organization and modification and gene expression regulation.
source: Genes underlying these correlations were significantly enriched in pathways involved in chromatin organization and modification and gene expression regulation.
evidence: Results from gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: DNM correlations were substantially attenuated in genes with lower expression and genes with frequent occurrences of LoF variants in the population.
source: The DNM correlations were substantially attenuated in genes with lower expression and genes with frequent occurrences of LoF variants in the population.
evidence: Summary of patterns observed in gene set-specific analyses.

claim: A similar attenuation of DNM correlations was observed in less pathogenic variant classes (e.g., synonymous variants).
source: A similar attenuation was observed in less pathogenic variant classes (e.g., synonymous variants).
evidence: Summary of patterns observed across variant classes.

claim: DNM enrichment correlations of five disorders were consistent with genetic correlations estimated from GWAS summary statistics (Spearman correlation = 0.70).
source: We also compared DNM enrichment correlations of five disorders with genetic correlations estimated from GWAS summary statistics (Supplementary file 1-STable 18). We had consistent findings from GWAS and DNM data (Spearman correlation = 0.70; Figure 5—figure supplement 8 and Supplementary file 1-STable 19).
evidence: Results from comparison of DNM and GWAS-based genetic correlations.

claim: EncoreDNM assumes probands from different input studies to be independent.
source: First, EncoreDNM assumes probands from different input studies to be independent.
evidence: Statement of a model assumption.

claim: When two studies have overlapping proband samples, enrichment correlation estimates may be inflated.
source: In rare cases when two studies have overlapping proband samples, enrichment correlation estimates may be inflated and must be interpreted with caution.
evidence: Logical inference about the effect of violating the independence assumption.

claim: Analysis of a typical pair of disorders with 18,000 genes takes about 10 min on a 2.5 GHz cluster with 1 core.
source: Analysis of a typical pair of disorders with 18,000 genes takes about 10 min on a 2.5 GHz cluster with 1 core.
evidence: Computational performance measurement.

claim: Synonymous variants were determined based on the 'synonymous SNV' annotation in ANNOVAR.
source: Synonymous variants were determined based on the 'synonymous SNV' annotation in ANNOVAR; Variants with 'startloss', 'stopgain', 'stoploss', 'splicing', 'frameshift insertion', 'frameshift deletion', or 'frameshift substitution' annotations were classified as LoF; Dmis variants were defined as nonsynonymous SNVs predicted to be deleterious by MetaSVM Dong et al., 2015; nonsynonymous SNVs predicted to be tolerable by MetaSVM were classified as Tmis.
evidence: Description of variant classification procedure.

claim: 18,454 autosomal protein-coding genes were included in the analysis.
source: We included 18,454 autosomal protein-coding genes in our analysis.
evidence: Description of the gene set used in the analysis.

claim: TTN was removed from the analysis due to its substantially larger size.
source: TTN was removed due to its substantially larger size.
evidence: Description of data processing decision.

claim: Genes with high/low probability of intolerance to LoF variants were defined using pLI scores.
source: First, we defined genes with high/low probability of intolerance to LoF variants using pLI scores (Karczewski et al., 2020), and identified genes with high/low brain expression (HBE/LBE) (Werling et al., 2020; Materials and methods; Supplementary file 1-STable 9).
evidence: Description of gene set definition using published scores.

claim: Genes with a high/low probability of intolerance to LoF variants (high-pLI/low-pLI) were defined as the 4,614 genes in the upper/lower quartiles of pLI scores.
source: Genes with a high/low probability of intolerance to LoF variants (high-pLI/low-pLI) were defined as the 4,614 genes in the upper/lower quartiles of pLI scores (Karczewski et al., 2020).
evidence: Specific definition of gene sets used in the analysis.

claim: Genes with high/low brain expression (HBE/LBE) were defined as the 4,614 genes in the upper/lower quartiles of expression in the human fetal brain.
source: Genes with high/low brain expression (HBE/LBE) were defined as the 4,614 genes in the upper/lower quartiles of expression in the human fetal brain (Werling et al., 2020).
evidence: Specific definition of gene sets used in the analysis.

claim: Genes with high/low heart expression (HHE/LHE) were defined as the 4,614 genes in the upper/lower quartiles of expression in the developing heart of embryonic mouse.
source: Genes with high/low heart expression (HHE/LHE) were defined as the 4,614 genes in the upper/lower quartiles of expression in the developing heart of embryonic mouse (Zaidi et al., 2013).
evidence: Specific definition of gene sets used in the analysis.

claim: Five biological pathways have been reported to be involved in congenital heart disease: chromatin remodeling, Notch signaling, cilia function, sarcomere structure and function, and RAS signaling.
source: Five biological pathways have been reported to be involved in congenital heart disease: chromatin remodeling, Notch signaling, cilia function, sarcomere structure and function, and RAS signaling (Zaidi and Brueckner, 2017).
evidence: Biological knowledge about CHD pathways, supported by citation.

claim: 1730 unique genes belong to the five CHD-related pathways.
source: We extracted 1730 unique genes that belong to these five pathways from the gene ontology database (Ashburner et al., 2000) and referred to the union set as CHD-related genes.
evidence: Description of gene set extraction from database.
